back: The study of the history, culture, nature and people of one specific place, and the practical use of this knowledge in museums, education and tourism.
The way a group of people remembers its past together; it decides which events, people and places are seen as important.
A visitor whose main reason to travel is to experience the history, culture and traditions of a place. Studied through demographics, motivations and psychological drivers.

front: Three evaluation criteria for heritage resources (Topic 3)
back: Integrity (how intact), significance (why important), authenticity (how truthful to the original). The seminar audit also uses accessibility.
An area shaped by the interaction of people and nature over time, seen as one whole rather than as separate objects.

front: Main parts of a funding proposal
back: Objectives, beneficiaries, activities, budget breakdown and timeline. The budget must be realistic.
Vision: a short picture of the desired future of a destination. Mission: its purpose and what it does to reach the vision.
Physical – maximum spatial density within safety limits. Ecological – reversible threshold of environmental and fabric damage. Social – crowding limit for visitor appreciation and resident comfort.
1 Define values (core assets) → 2 Set indicators (abrasion, humidity) → 3 Fix standards (critical limits) → 4 Take action (entry caps, routing).
Timed entry reservation (hourly quotas), dynamic tariff pricing (peak-hour prices shift demand), spatial micro-zoning (fragile core vs. buffer zones).
Significance assessment (mapping OUV), vulnerability analysis (environmental and human risks), policy formulation (restoration and usage protocols).
IoT climate sensors (humidity, vibration), heatmap crowd tracking via Wi-Fi telemetry (bottlenecks), BIM digital twins (predicting structural strain and wear).

"Through interpretation, understanding; through understanding, appreciation; through appreciation, protection." Interpretation reveals meanings through first-hand experience, not just facts.
Human connection (personal struggles over timelines), universal themes (local history linked to global values), provocative arc (raise questions, not dry answers).
Living heritage: territory over trophy cases (heritage in its original setting), community ownership (residents as narrators), focus on intangible traditions (crafts, folklore, oral history).

front: Four steps of an interpretive plan
back: 1 Asset audit → 2 Theme framing (big-idea statement) → 3 Medium selection (guides, signage, AR/VR, workshops) → 4 Visitor evaluation (emotional resonance, retention).
Heritage products should be holistic, immersive and place-based, with emotional connection, narrative design and cultural and human elements in the tour package.
Cultural explorers – depth and accuracy. Experience seekers – visuals, atmosphere, shareability. Family groups – interactive learning, games, accessible amenities.
Cultural preservation (authenticity, carrying capacity, community respect) vs. commercial growth (monetization, audience expansion, reinvestment in conservation).
Dynamic pricing for off-peak visits, exclusive night tours, off-season (winter) festivals.

International (treaties, soft-law conventions) → National (statutes, registries) → State/regional (preservation offices, park districts) → Local (zoning, historic district commissions, building codes).
Venice Charter 1964 – authenticity and integrity. UNESCO World Heritage Convention 1972 – OUV, cultural and natural. ICOMOS Cultural Tourism Charter 1999 – visitor management, host communities.
Voluntary, binding agreement restricting development rights forever. Property stays private; restrictions pass to future buyers; owners get tax deductions. Limitation: needs owner consent.

front: Overlay zoning and Certificate of Appropriateness
back: Overlay zoning: special rules over existing zoning for scale, materials, alterations. Certificate of Appropriateness: mandatory review of exterior changes in historic zones.

front: National Register: what it does and its limit
back: Official list of historic places; gives recognition and financial incentives. Listing alone does not restrict private owners unless federal funding or permits are involved.
Economic driver (GDP, jobs, multipliers), commercialization risk (overtourism, costs, displacement), sustainable balance (revenue aligned with conservation and social equity).
1.8x–2.5x on average: every $1 invested in heritage conservation yields up to $2.50 in indirect regional returns.

front: Four pillars of sustainable heritage management
back: Carrying capacity limits, adaptive reuse models, re-investive revenue loops (earmarked visitor taxes), community co-governance (shared decisions and profits).
1 Assessment (integrity, significance) → 2 Co-design (community) → 3 Retrofitting (eco-efficiency without losing identity) → 4 Operations (self-sustaining activities).
40% site conservation and restoration, 30% local community and infrastructure fund, 20% visitor management and education, 10% administration.

front: Four core formats of heritage events
back: Cultural festivals (living traditions), reenactments (on-site reconstructions), exhibitions (curated narratives around artifacts), installations (temporary artistic interventions).
Research → Co-design → Logistics (permits, staging, crowd routing) → Delivery (live interpretation, flow) → Legacy (site restoration, impact review).
Co-creation, educational depth, living evolution vs. commercial packaging of rituals, frozen stereotypes, resident alienation.
Object-centered (materiality, expert monopoly, passive visitor) vs. experience-centered (performance, co-creation, affectivity – emotions govern perception).
Affirmation (reinforcing values), empathy (connecting with past lives), re-evaluation (discomfort from difficult truths).
1 Expectation (memory baggage) → 2 Encounter (embodied, sensory) → 3 Resonance (emotion tests the narrative) → 4 Meaning (renewed stance in the present).
Sensory and interactive engagement: immersive storytelling, augmented reality, food heritage and participatory methods that raise engagement and reinforce identity.

front: Four trends shaping the future of heritage tourism
back: Climate change, digitalization, inclusivity and community empowerment – each brings challenges and opportunities.
